Enforce named shapes on estimates and interval endpoints

Source: R/shape-intervals.R
shape_intervals.Rd

Apply shape-enforcing operators to an existing estimate and its lower and upper endpoints. Construction and calibration of the initial uncertainty remain the caller's responsibility.

Usage

shape_intervals(
  estimate,
  lower,
  upper,
  data,
  constraints,
  interval = c("simultaneous", "pointwise"),
  level = 0.95
)

Arguments

estimate, lower, upper

finite numeric vectors, one value per row of data. The lower endpoints must not exceed the upper endpoints.

data

a data frame of finite numeric coordinates. Rows may be in any order but must form a complete Cartesian product without duplicates. Coordinates may be irregularly spaced. A single coordinate gives a curve.

constraints

a named list, with coordinate names as names and character vectors of restrictions as elements. Codes are "m+" (nondecreasing), "m-" (nonincreasing), "c+" (convex), "c-" (concave), and "+" (nonnegative). Curvature restrictions may occur in at most one coordinate. Monotonicity may be imposed in several coordinates. Positivity applies to the function, regardless of which coordinate carries its code.

interval

character; whether the input is a "simultaneous" band or "pointwise" limits. This describes the input, and does not calibrate it.

level

numeric; the nominal level of the input, strictly between zero and one.

Value

A tibble containing data, .estimate, .lower_ci, and .upper_ci, in the original row order. The interval_info attribute records the operator, restrictions, input interval type and coverage scope. Standard errors and Gaussian critical values are not recalculated.

Details

The operator first thresholds at zero if requested, then sorts each monotone coordinate in the order given by constraints, then takes the greatest convex minorant in the curvature coordinate. Concavity uses the negative of the greatest convex minorant of the negative values. The minorant uses actual coordinate distances. Sorting gives equal mass to each grid coordinate, including on irregular grids; it does not approximate Lebesgue-weighted rearrangement on such grids.

These finite-grid operators preserve order, leave a function with the requested shapes unchanged, and do not increase maximum absolute distance. Consequently, whenever the entire initial band contains a target with the requested shapes on the grid, the transformed band also contains it. Its maximum width cannot increase. This is a deterministic statement about a whole-grid event; it does not guarantee nominal pointwise coverage after transforming pointwise limits. Nor does it correct smoothing bias or an invalid initial uncertainty calculation. For a posterior supported on the restricted functions the analogous event inclusion applies to posterior probability; this operation does not construct that posterior.

The guarantees concern values on the supplied grid. Linear interpolation of curves, or multilinear interpolation on rectangles, also has the named directional shapes between grid points. The output is not a fitted spline and need not obey coefficient inequalities, centring, integral constraints, or other equalities. Use shape_confidence_set() to represent intersections with such restrictions. Several curvature coordinates are unsupported: sequential directional convexification need not preserve earlier convexity. Extreme numeric ranges that prevent reliable slope comparisons or interpolation in double precision produce an error.

References

Chernozhukov, V., Fernandez-Val, I. and Galichon, A. (2009). Improving point and interval estimators of monotone functions by rearrangement. Biometrika, 96, 559–575. doi:10.1093/biomet/asp030 .

Chen, X., Chernozhukov, V., Fernandez-Val, I., Kostyshak, S. and Luo, Y. (2021). Shape-Enforcing Operators for Generic Point and Interval Estimators of Functions. Journal of Machine Learning Research, 22(220), 1–42. https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v22/20-513.html.

Examples

x <- c(0, 0.1, 0.4, 0.8, 1)
f <- c(0.1, 0.4, 0.2, 0.9, 0.7)
shape_intervals(f, f - 0.3, f + 0.3, data.frame(x = x),
  constraints = list(x = c("+", "m+")))
#> # A tibble: 5 x 4
#>       x .estimate .lower_ci .upper_ci
#>   <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1   0         0.1       0         0.4
#> 2   0.1       0.2       0         0.5
#> 3   0.4       0.4       0.1       0.7
#> 4   0.8       0.7       0.4       1  
#> 5   1         0.9       0.6       1.2
